posts.headline: The Fed held rates steady again
posts.caption:
The Fed left rates where they are.

Your savings account keeps paying what it pays.
Your credit card keeps charging what it charges.
Nothing on your statement changes this month.

My take: the waiting is the hard part, and it is not over.

Has a rate decision ever changed a plan of yours?

Source: Federal Reserve statement

posts.headline: Where prices actually moved
posts.caption:
Inflation cooled, but not in the aisle you shop in.

Headline prices rose 2.9% over the year.
Groceries rose faster than the month before.
Rent is still the biggest line in most budgets.

My take: an average is not a receipt, and the average is not what you pay.

Which line in your budget moved most this year?

Source: BLS Consumer Price Index

#Inflation #Groceries #CostOfLiving

posts.headline: The 30-year mortgage rate, six months on
posts.caption:
Mortgage rates have drifted down for six months.

The 30-year average is near 6.3%.
On a $400,000 loan, that is roughly $180 a month less than April.
House prices have not moved with it.

My take: this helps buyers at the margin, not the ones priced out.

Are you watching rates, or watching prices?

Source: Freddie Mac weekly survey
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Mortgage #Housing #Rates

posts.headline: What a one-bedroom costs across six metros
posts.caption:
The same apartment, six very different prices.

New York asks about three times what Houston asks.
None of these include utilities or parking.
Moving for cheaper rent usually means moving for a different salary too.

My take: compare rent as a share of local pay, never as a raw number.

What share of your pay goes to rent?

Source: Rental listing aggregates

#Rent #CostOfLiving #Housing

posts.headline: Card balance or emergency fund?
posts.caption:
One spare $500, two reasonable homes for it.

Paying the card stops interest at about 24.6% a year.
Saving it earns about 4.3% a year.
The maths favours the card; the peace of mind favours the fund.

My take: a small buffer first, then everything at the card.

Which one would you do?

Source: Federal Reserve G.19, FDIC
Educational only — not financial advice.

posts.headline: How a port strike reaches your receipt
posts.caption:
A strike at the docks ends up in your grocery bill.

Ships wait offshore instead of unloading.
Retailers ration whatever stock they already hold.
Scarcity turns into a higher sticker price.

My take: the lag is usually weeks, so the bill arrives after the headlines stop.

Have you noticed anything missing from your shelves lately?

Source: Port authority notices

posts.headline: A major payments processor is down
posts.caption:
A payments processor outage is hitting card terminals.

Some card payments are being delayed or declined.
Retail shares slipped on the news.
This is developing and the cause is not confirmed.

My take: carry a little cash on days like this — not as a strategy, just as a backup.
